To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) fungal taxa in indoor air vary both in taxa, concentration and seasonal variation in different residences and regions; (2) the fungal taxa in indoor environments were similar to those of outdoor air; (3) indoor fungal species were associated with asthma and allergic symptoms; and (4) fungal taxa in outdoor air were similar to those in indoor environments, and were associated with asthma symptoms and allergic symptoms in asthmatic children

1) the most common fungal genera in the homes of the studied children were Aspergillus, Penicillium and Cladosporium; 2) the most common species were A. versicolor and P. brevicompactum, and 3) the most common genera in the homes were Penicillium, Aspergillus and Cladosporiium.
the fungal species present are different in the homes of children with asthma compared to the homes of children without asthma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the indoor fungal species and the identification of the fungal species in the homes of children with asthma.
the identification of the fungi present in homes, the quantification of the fungal load, and the correlation of the fungal load with the presence of asthma and allergy.
understanding the relationship between indoor fungal species and asthmatic symptoms in children, and with developing a method of identifying fungal species in the indoor air of children's residences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the indoor fungal diversity and composition is influenced by a complex interaction of several factors including climate, building characteristics, ventilation, humidity, and the presence of pets.
there are a number of fungal species that are more commonly found in the homes of children with asthma than in the homes of healthy children.
the fungal species found in the homes of children with asthma are not the same as those found in the homes without asthma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fungal species in the homes of children in the U.S. are diverse.
the most common fungal species in the homes of our asthmatic children are Cladosporium spp. (30.8%), Aspergillus spp. (22.4%), Penicillium spp. (21.2%) and Alternaria spp. (20%).
the fungal diversity in the homes of children with asthma was similar to the diversity found in the homes of healthy children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fungal species present indoors can be quite different in different homes.

the fungal taxa that are most commonly found indoors vary from one geographic region to another, and that the most common indoor fungal species are also the most commonly reported as causing allergy or infection.
fungal exposures are highly variable in homes and are likely to contribute to the development of asthma.
